utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you said something that was not correct. The putrefying liquids because of the gravity seeped to the bottom and they would wet the part of the clothing that was underneath on the surface and that that putrefaction liquid dilutes the dye in the clothing and then it is -- it seeps out. As for whether an expert had a view about this or not, what I'm saying is that the body -- the dye comes from that because it corresponds to the contours of the body. I don't think that you need to have much other expert knowledge to be able to deduce something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your reasoning is that only there where the body was directly on the clothes and on the soil, that only there the colour of the clothing taken by the putrefaction liquid would then come on to the soil. And now have you considered the possibility that the colour of the clothing, without the -- well, let's say without the help of the body liquids, the putrefying liquids could enter the soil. You link -- you link the- could I say- the drainage of the colour of the clothing to the putrefying process. Do you have any knowledge about similar drainage of colour from clothing without a body on top of it? I mean, if I would just put, for example, jeans somewhere in the same position without a body on it, would the colour of the jeans not enter the soil underneath? Do you have any knowledge of that or any experience of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have experience from other such exhumations. When, however, the clothing is not pressed down by something heavy, it would not leave such a clear contour of, let's say, jeans as we do have. Where you have the clothing adhering to the ground firmly, you would also have probably some dyeing or perhaps not. However, in this case where the body was firmly pressed to the ground by the rock, we got this clear coloured contour of the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it seems to me that apart from the weight on the clothing and weight on the body, that it allows you also to give us a time estimate on how long it should have been there. Could you explain to me whether -- why this would have taken such a long time, why it would not have been possible to have the same result in a couple of days or -- what makes you conclude that this colouring of the soil must have taken the time you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not gauge the time only on the basis of the colouration, also on the basis of the decomposition of the body when the water-levels, for instance, rose and then when they dropped. Based on the estimation of the putrefaction of the body and on the basis of the colouration of the soil beneath the body, I provided my opinion that the body had been there for several weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time the colouration of the soil seems to be one of the relevant factors. What basis have you concluded that the colouration of the soil supports the conclusion that the body must have been there for a longer time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this was indeed an important element, the colouration of the ground, but it -- there are also the other factors. Don't forget that the rock was over the body, not to the full extent but to some extent indeed and it firmly pressed the body on to the ground, so much so that we were forced to cut part of the rock. Colouration is an important element for this evaluation, but not only that. We also took into account all the other factors. And I'm referring specifically to this case at hand, this particular body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, at the same time colouration being an important factor, what is known? Is there anything known about the speed of colouration of soil on which a body with some weight on it is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything specific about it. My conclusion was based on the experience I had at the time and on -- and the experience I gained later on when I was participating in the exhumation at Batajnica, as well as some exhumation processes I performed during the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then take it that when you're referring to your experience, that you're telling us that in similar situations where it was known that the bodies had been in situ for a longer period of time that you saw similar colouration of the soil. Is that how I should understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also that in situations where it was known that bodies had not been for a long period of time in that situation that the colouration of the soil was less or perhaps non-existent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In -- it was present only in some places and not as was the case in this particular instance where it reflected the -- the contours of the entire body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Just to follow-up a bit. Professor Aleksandric, you indicated that the -- the saponification process and the discolouration of the body was one indicator of the length of time that the body had been stuck under -- near -- underneath the rocks. I just want to draw your attention to paragraph 168 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I believe Ms. Issa's misspoken herself, not the discolouration process, but rather the decomposition process, which is a distinct issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I believe the witness's testimony was in part that the discolouration caused by the saponification is an indicator -- perhaps I should use the word saponification, Your Honour, of the length of time that the body had been present underneath the rocks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know what was discoloured, the clothing or the body, at least fluids play a role there but perhaps you clarify that so that there's --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: The saponification process which ultimately led to the discolouration of the soil underneath the body as you described earlier, you've indicated was one indicator to you as to the length of time that the body had been stuck underneath the rocks. I draw your attention to paragraph 168 of your statement, and in part you say, when you're describing saponification --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I don't know if the interpretation was good or not. It seems to me you said the discolouration of the soil. There was no discolouration. In fact, there was colouration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Issa, you used the word "discolouration," which I understand is to -- that the colour disappears. I also can imagine that discolouration would mean that the colour changes. So discolouration seems to be not an unequivocal term, and that might at this moment cause the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'll be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: What I'm referring to, Professor Aleksandric, is the process that you -- that we've seen earlier in the video and that you describe whereby once the body was removed the -- the colour on the clothing had been transferred to the soil, which -- depicting a bluish/greenish colour, as you've earlier described, and you've indicated that that was one indicator as to the length of time that the body had been present underneath the soil. I also just would like to draw your attention to the bottom part of paragraph 168 in which you are describing the saponification of body 20 and you also say that this: "Is a process of decomposition where the soft tissue of a body converts into soap, but if it get wets and you touch it, it begins to foam which is why we get remains which represent a more shapeless mass which still shows a leg and which has not been moved from its previous position." I'd just like to refer you to Exhibit P -- P513. While we wait for the correct exhibit to come up - that's not the correct exhibit - I just want to ask you if you can explain and just elaborate on that statement. Why is the fact of a more shapeless mass an indicator that assists in identifying the length of time that -- that the body was present?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall the first photographs, for instance, this one, yes, excellent, you can clearly see the contours of the body here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: For the record, that's P512. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can clearly see the contours of the body. The process of saponification is such where the matter in the tissue transforms into soap. When you try and when you start manipulating such a body, it becomes a slimy mass. And you can see that clearly in the earlier photographs where you had bodies on a table, where you weren't able to see the clear contours of the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And why is it that this process is an indicator of the length of time that the body was present underneath the rocks?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking into account the process of putrefaction or of saponification, taking into account the weather conditions, the external temperatures, whether the body was partly in moist conditions or partly perhaps in dry conditions, as I've already explained, on the basis of our experience we make an assessment as to how long that body could have been at a particular site, and that was the assessment I gave --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We were initially discussing the process of saponification and the question was directed towards saponification. The answer has now taken into account a number of different factors, including putrification, which is, if I'm not mistaken, a different process which creates different issues. And I'm hoping we can get some clarification in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the attention has been drawn to paragraph 168 by Ms. Issa, which reads: "Saponification is a particular process of putrification ..." So therefore to say that it's a different matter seems not to be correctly on the basis of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate what is in the 92 ter statement, however I think with regard to this issue because there are so many different actual scientific factors that are going to contribute to the Chamber's understanding of what's going on, that it may be of some assistance to see whether or not there is some clarity that can be drawn with regard to the issue of saponification as opposed to the generalised notion of putrification when dealing with a body found in the kind of condition that this body was found. If you don't find it to be of assistance, so be it, but I think ultimately it's going to be of some concern, to not only the Chamber but also to an understanding of the ultimate issue which we need an answer to which is: How long this body was in situ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, two observations. First, if you consider what the witness in his 92 ter statement said, that is, that saponification is a specific part of the process of putrification, then you can put that to him in cross-examination. Further, the circumstances the witness describes are, to some extent, directly known to him because he has been on the spot and can, for example, see whether it was dry at that time or whether there were any marks of a higher water-level at an earlier stage whether -- I mean, there are a lot of matters, perhaps not everything. The witness might not have been fully aware of the climate and the water-level at any moment. But certainly I can see the matters you're raising, they are perfectly suitable for cross-examination, but not at this moment to object to the questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And just to wrap up this point, Professor, you've indicated that it was your assessment that this body had been there for a long time. You also said it had been there for several weeks. Can you be more specific as to what you mean by "long time"?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said, "long time," I meant several weeks. One cannot be more precise than that, but certainly not less than four or five weeks under the conditions in which the body was found. I don't think I have to go into that again. I've explained that already.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Moving then on to bodies R-18 and R-32. R-18 was ultimately identified as Ilira Frrokaj and R-32 remains unidentified. You say in photograph 229 of your statement that R-32 was found at about 200 metres downstream in the water stuck in the mud. And in paragraph 231 of your statement you describe that next to the car where body 18 was found, you found a big part of a skull but at the time you didn't know whether they belonged to body 18, "so we placed them in the same body-bag". After the autopsy and anthropological analysis, you say that you conclude that this part of the skull did not belong to body 18, so you marked it 18-I or 18-1 because it was packed together with 18. I'd like to just show you a couple of short clips and then I'm going to ask you a few questions. Exhibit 452, starting at 013537.1, if you can indicate what is that first image that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the best view of the right leg of the body. The entire position is marked with number 18, that's at the beginning of the natural part of the canyon. Next to a vehicle that was found near the body, if you played the footage you'll see that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side there was a part of the skull which --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: We're not receiving any interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I don't hear the witness speak at this moment either, so I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I think he stopped at which --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you just continue what you were saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last thing we heard from you was: "On the other side there was a part of the skull which ..." Can you please continue from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which can be seen if we play the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Footage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you see number 18, and here in the centre of the still we can see the top part of the skull.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's at 013553.5. If we can then just continue playing, please. There. If we can then go to the next clip, which starts at 013728.6.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The skull was placed into the same body-bag with the body. The number was moved from the car on to the ground here in order to be clearly visible in the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And just shortly before 013733.2, we see you taking what appears to be a skull and placing it there on the ground. Can you just indicate what you did there and why?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely the part of the skull that you saw on the other side of the vehicle, I placed next to the body in order to transfer it together with the body into the body-bag. Subsequently this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And if we then --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If we can just continue playing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. If we then go to Exhibit P511, please. Just the middle photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you indicate what that photograph depicts, Professor Aleksandric?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The skull that you saw placed together with body number 18 in the earlier still. After a forensic and anthropological analysis, it was concluded that the isolated part of the skull did not belong to body number 18. During the autopsy we gave it a new label, 18/1. During the autopsy of the body marked R-32 - and this is something we did with the other bodies as well - we established that parts of the bone of the skull belonging to body 32, and this is the body that you saw marked as R-32 and which is shown by this tweezer, that the part along which there was a fracture is fully matched with the part of the skull marked R-18/1. In other words, the two parts of the skull belong to the same person, and that's R-32. Furthermore, this means that the body marked R-32 was initially at the beginning of the canyon that a part of the skull, since it was crushed, remained in the beginning part of the canyon and that the water current bore with it most of the bodies so that the body of R-32 along with some parts of the skull were found down there at the very end of the natural canyon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can just very briefly then go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one thing. You have, therefore, excluded that part of R-32, that small portion of that bone, has been moved by any other means upstream a couple of hundred metres and then was found -- you understand what I mean? You are taking the natural cause of the body being taken by the water as the explanation and you have excluded another possible explanation, that is, that part of the body found downstream was transported by whatever means to a place higher up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course this cannot be ruled out, absolutely. However, under the circumstances in which you have some body parts found at the end of the canyon, you can conclude that R-32 was washed down. And this is more logical than concluding that somebody took a part of the skull of R-18, which was together with body R-32, and took it upstream in order to leave it at the initial part of the canyon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit P544, and we can just look at the middle photograph, that obviously depicts R-32. And I just -- just to -- if you can just confirm that for the record, Professor Aleksandric.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see a wire that goes through the body -- through the damage which was established in the autopsy and which was inflicted by the passage of a projectile. We did not have a large probe to show this and we used a piece of wire instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. And it appears that this body is only partly decomposed and seems to have some flesh remaining on it. Are you able to provide an estimate, approximate estimate, as to how long the body was -- was in the water?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to estimate that, and the question is whether the body was in the water, immersed in the water all the time. It may have been on dry land and then ended up in the water, it is difficult to give an estimation but definitely it must have been there for several weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And can you be -- you're unable to be specific as to what you mean by several weeks?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, at least four to five weeks, perhaps a week less. We can't assert with any certainty that the body was in the water all the time. It may have been on dry land for some time and then two weeks prior to its recovery it was thrown into the water.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to move on to a group of bodies, R-21, -22, -23, -24, and -25 which are described as shoes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' -- just for the record -- for Your Honours' information, paragraphs 174, 176, and 189, 190, in the statement are -- appear to be objected to and are at issue by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, we see the locations of these bodies as focused on the screen. I'd like to just turn to the video, 452, and I'm going to play it through and then ask you some questions. That's at 015659.3.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. We can just pause it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: At 015730.5, we see a label of number 25. Can you just indicate briefly where that was found in relation to the canyon.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw from this footage that we had first a very steep vertical part of the canyon some 20 metres high and then another part which stood at an angle of roughly 45 degrees, which is overgrown by vegetation and also some 20 metres high. Immediately before the part of the canyon which is free of vegetation and which means that occasionally water flows through there, some 10 metres beyond this shoe a group of bodies was found. You will see as you will play the video that the shoe was found some 3 metres away from the bottom, and down there the other shoe was found, the shoe belonging to this same pair.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If we can then just continue playing the footage, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the group of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Stop there, please. Just rewind it slightly. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So this is the group of bodies. We can perhaps just continue playing it, that's at 05746 [sic]. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can start explaining right away, this is the lower part of the body in trousers, this is number 24. To the right of the body is number R-23, but you cannot see it very well and that's a whole body --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's at 05756.1 [sic].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now there is the next body and at the beginning you can see a cone at the top with a number 22 meaning that is a another body. I think that they are zooming in now so that you would be able to see the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's at 015811.1. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you followed, you will see that the group of bodies is in the direction -- the same direction as the pair of shoes that were found. Now that's what's being indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: We can stop there, please, that's at 015829.5. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now you will see --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the right of this group of bodies, there was the upper part of the body marked R-21. And if you continue showing this, I think you will be able to see it better because the shot was interrupted when the camera focused on upstream, so then we will see what the situation was downstream.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the upper part of the body marked R-21.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's at 015917.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And when you refer to the upper part of the body, just to clarify, in your statement you state that it was found that R-21 and R-24 were, in fact, the same person. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the site we found the upper and the lower part of the body at a relatively small distance apart, 2 to 3 metres. So the association at the location was that the top or the upper part of the body marked as R-21 and the lower part of the body R-24 possibly could belong to the same person. After an analysis and an anthropological analysis, we concluded that the two -- the upper and the lower part of the body do belong to one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If we can then please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now you can see the relationship of the other bodies to each other, 22, 23, and 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay and that was at about 015924.2, just for the record. If we can then go -- start.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: We could stop there for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is that -- we're looking at body 23. Can you just indicate, is that -- did you just mention earlier that that was a whole body or part of a body?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 23 and 22 were whole bodies. 21 was the upper part of the body and 24 was the lower part of the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: We can then just continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you heard my voice where I was dictating my findings into a Dictaphone. I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. And the video -- just that clip stopped at 020018.0 for the record. Now, Professor Aleksandric, you say in your statement, in your 92 ter statement, at paragraph 176 that the video shows: "The shoes I mentioned which led us to believe that at least one person was thrown down from the top of the hill and also a body could be seen downhill from where the shoes were located. The shoe was marked with R-25." In 177 you say that: "We believed that the shoe found higher up belonged to the body parts of which were separated, 21 and 24, because body 21 had a shoe on. This shoe was marked R-25. Next to body R-23, one shoe of a different type was found." My question to you is: Can you elaborate or further explain based on your observations and the steepness of the canyon and the vegetation if -- if this is consistent with or inconsistent with bodies being pushed or thrown down the canyon?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say right away that there is a mistake here. Paragraph 177 says because there was a -- body 21 had a shoe on, but it actually should say body 22 had a shoe on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that when you read the later paragraphs where it is -- says that 22 had one shoe on, but body 21 had shoes and next to body 23 a shoe was found very near the actual foot. So I'm speaking about our impressions in situ. And then later only we came to the conclusion that body 21 and body 24 were one and the same body. In situ that was just our working hypothesis. Now, bodies 22 and 23 had shoes on and above in the growth you found shoes. We went by the logic that those shoes could have belonged either to body 24 or body 21. I repeat at that time we had not yet come to the conclusion that those two parts belonged to the same person. The other thing is since a pair of shoes was found higher up in the vegetation, it's evident that the water never reaches as far as that vegetation. And under the assumption that nobody took the shoes from the actual location and threw them up into the grass, it would be logical that the body was first in that vegetated area and then later it dropped lower. In other words, the body from the top of the canyon, from the top of the slope, that's where it came from. If you find the whole group of bodies in the same place and one body has lost its shoes, then our conclusion was that perhaps the whole group of people at that point in time, we were thinking whether it was three or four bodies because it could have been logical also to think that the water, the stream, the current, took the top part of 24 or the lower part of 21, so it could have been two people. So it was just our working hypothesis only that 21 and 24 were part of the one and the same body. If you came up to that image, it could easily have been assumed that the whole group of bodies had come down from the top of the canyon and that it first dropped to the part that was covered with vegetation where one of the bodies lost its shoes, and then later they rolled down to the place where the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what particularly indicates to this is practically the straight line from where the -- of where the bodies were found and where the shoes were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean the shoes were not together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not together. One was found 3 metres away from the one where we zoomed in on the shot. It would be the other shoe of that same pair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where you say the straight line, you mean the line where the body was found -- or at least part of the body was found, the first shoe, and the second shoe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second shoe and then all the way to the top. If you noticed, I didn't say that they were thrown or pushed. I said that they ended up in the place where they were found from the top of the canyon. How they got there is something that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I didn't, as Your Honour indicated, raise an objection before the explanation was given but that was the reason for the objection initially was the speculative nature and the assumptions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness himself already said a couple of times that he doesn't know certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means he sticks fairly well to what his expertise tells him and what was working hypothesis or assumptions. So the Chamber will certainly clearly make a distinction between expert findings and assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Issa, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that you have in mind one hour for the next witness. If we would have a break now, there would remain another 70 minutes so you would well stay in your estimate. But I just draw your attention to it that we are coming close to the moment where after the break there would be only one hour left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm actually -- I just have maybe about 10 or 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then you have not an hour left for the next witness. You're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Actually, I'll try and wrap up very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you said after the break, half an hour. I know I interrupted you a couple of times, but certainly not for three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'll try and wrap up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Professor Aleksandric, just very briefly and quickly at paragraph 244 of your statement, you discuss the fact that there was a missile that exploded on the 15th of September, 1998, at the Lake Radonjic canal area where you were working. And then you say at the end of that paragraph that: "We had the impression that somebody saw us working in the canal, positioned us precisely, and informed those who then shelled us at our exact location." Can you just indicate what is the basis of that opinion or conclusion? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because somebody who fired at us from a mortar, and we were told that it was a mortar by the experienced policemen who had been in combat there for months, if somebody determines the exact position where a large number of us were, a large group of people, and fortunately for us the shell overreached and missed us and it hit higher up above us. But it was enough to see the dust flying up. Then it would be logical to assume that nobody was just firing indiscriminately or at random but they had the exact coordinates that they could have received from someone who could have determined the exact coordinates where we were by observing us. Don't forget that it's a forested area up there. It's not a nice forest. It's more like a jungle and it's very easy to take cover and conceal oneself up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more questions. Was there anything about the crime scene itself when you were working over the course of those days, Professor Aleksandric, that indicated to you that it was either staged or set up as a crime scene and that it was not a true crime scene?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's exactly the other way around. Everything indicated that the location next to the canyon, the dry part of the canyon on the slope was precisely the place of execution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you observe anything out of the ordinary, either in the behaviour of the police or anything else that indicated to you that this could have been a staged scene and not a true crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question as asked. It calls for speculation. It's certainly outside the qualifications of the witness. He's not a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It also deals with how many -- you know, how many police officers, where were they located, what time of the day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's all fine, but Ms. Issa is entitled to ask whether the witness observed anything out of the ordinary. And then she gives a clue as to what kind of out of the ordinary, which is I would say -- is not inadmissible because it anticipates on the position clearly taken by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It also makes -- it also makes it leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not inadmissible. Please proceed. Could you tell us whether there was anything out of the ordinary which you focused -- which you observed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing unusual. Nothing special, either in the behaviour of the people, nothing in particular. But it was -- there was some degree of horror at what we had found. The bodies were not piled on top of one other. As you were able to see from the degrees some bodies, like 2 and 9, were on the surface, but the majority of the other bodies were intermingled with the soil, probably due to the course of time and because of rain and -- because when it rains there, it rains quite hard. Stones and pebbles moved, soil moved, and that's how the bodies came to be intermingled with the soil. And as I said, we found piles of gravel. When we found them, it was evident that those mounds of gravel were formed by hand. It was not something that was formed naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for me to understand, is that what you usually find if you find bodies, that -- I do not fully understand what you mean to say by this was made by hand, by man, rather than --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mound of gravel where we found body 14 and 15, that mound could not be naturally formed by atmospheric occurrences. The same thing would also apply to body 10. 14 and 15 were completely covered by gravel in the form of a cone or a mound. Body 10 as well. Perhaps the earth had washed away from the gravel because of the rain, so with body number 10 you were able to see the bones through. So they were obvious immediately when you looked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And finally, Professor Aleksandric, did you observe anything about the crime scene that indicated to you that the bodies had been placed there deliberately by the Serbs or Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very composite question. Whether the bodies were put there, by whom they were put there, these are separate questions, Ms. Issa. By the way, if the first question is answered in a negative, the second question -- there's no need to put it anymore. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you observe anything about the crime scene that led you to believe that the Serbian authorities had anything to do with the creation of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Same objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not up to me to establish that or to think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... outside of his expertise and is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not necessarily outside of the expertise of the witness. It depends also a bit on his answer, Mr. Guy-Smith. But, Ms. Issa, the question is put perhaps in a too limited way. Because you asked whether the witness observed anything about the crime scene that led him to believe, I would rather ask him whether he noticed anything at the crime scene which could have been understood as an indication that the bodies had been moved to this place rather than that the bodies were bodies of persons that died at the place where the bodies were found, apart from, of course, the water stream. If you heard my answer, could you please answer it -- my question, could you please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the place that was outside the canal. It was on the slope or are you asking generally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking generally, but you don't have to respond to the possible replacement dislocation of bodies due to the water because we have dealt with that. So that is bodies being put there by any other means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Taking into account the wounds determined by the autopsy - and I said out of the nine bodies found on the surface or immediately below the surface, we had seven with projectile wounds, and in view of the fact how the bodies were intermingled with the soil and taking into account the damages from the projectiles on both walls of the canal, my conclusion would be that the majority of the bodies were liquidated there by fire-arms. But you cannot determine whether this happened at the same time. However, body number 1, which was partly in a nylon bag and partly in a jute bag, and there was no projectile damage on either of the bags, you could conclude that that body had been brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm specifically asking for indications for bodies brought there, not for conclusions on how people may have died in that place. But the you say this -- the bodies that were in a bag you would consider it a -- an indication for the possibility that the body was put there. Do you have any other indications for bodies to have been put there when not alive anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I could say that definitely only for body number 1. As for the other bodies, I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's refrain from speculation. Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Aleksandric, I have one question for you, and you don't have to say a lot about it. A simple yes or no would do. During your investigation on site, did you pay any attention to the presence of insect or -- I take it that you call it larvae of insects on the bodies or on the clothing? Did you consider that? Did you describe that because we have not perhaps received all the information. Was that part of the investigation? If you say yes, then we'll -- or if you say no, we would just like to know without further details at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't say yes or no. We did not find any larvae or worms or flies or anything like that. If we had found any, we would have also included that in our autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Aleksandric, for various reasons this Chamber has decided that cross-examination, that is, examination by the Defence, will take place at a later stage. The date still has to be arranged. So therefore, unfortunately, we have to ask you to come back when you are there -- when the time is there. At the same time, as you may have noticed, there is a report from French experts. As soon as an English translation is available, it will be sent to you. Would you then be so kind to, as soon as possible, to respond in writing or to comment in writing on the findings and the reasoning in those reports. Would you be willing to do that? And we note that you are back only on the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, but I will be able to do that only in late August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that. Then, Professor Aleksandric, I'd first of all like to thank you very much for coming to the Hague and to answer all the questions that were put to you. At the same time, I would like to instruct you not to discuss with others, even talk with others, about the testimony you have given or you are still about to give because cross-examination still has to follow. You understand that instruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then thank you very much. You are excused and you'll further hear from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Issa, we'll have a break for 20 minutes and then there are 55 minutes remaining for you for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- Just to indicate, Mr. Dutertre will be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll then tell him that he's got 55 minutes. We'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, would you please sit down for a second because I have to deal with a procedural issue before we start. The Chamber has studied the lengthy or the huge number of matters in which the parties could not disagree. Some disappointment came into our mind, but we have reviewed the 92 ter statement. Where this statement contains an opinion which - and I'm talking about the 92 ter statement of Professor Dunjic - which goes beyond his direct experience and is prejudicial to the Defence or if it's purely speculative or it represents hearsay upon hearsay that is obviously of no value whatsoever, then we have struck the passages and the remaining passages of the questionable evidentiary value may be clarified in direct examination or in cross-examination and will be given the weight they deserve in the Chamber's discretion, which could well be no weight at all. I give you the passages which are struck. Paragraph 77, the highlighted portion; paragraph 122, highlighted portion; 131; 339; 365; 454; 480; 481; 579; last two sentences of 710, starting: "One of the victim's bodies had a ring ..." Until the end of that paragraph; and 713. This is not to say that a proper foundation could not be laid during the examination of the witness, but there's insufficient basis in the -- in the statement. On one point we had some doubts, that's 57: "The body was dumped and hidden in a cement sewage canal situated between the hangars of this Ekonomija farm." The Chamber reading and understanding this portion as this body was found in a not easy visible place in a cement sewage canal situated between the hangars of this Ekonomija farm, that's how we understood this and not as a direct -- an expression of direct knowledge of dumping or an intent to hide. And this might guide the parties as well in how the Chamber reads, that is, not only literally but always contextually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's quite helpful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Professor Dunjic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. Would you please make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Dunjic. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Dutertre, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Dutertre, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As regards Professor Dunjic, the Prosecution has prepared a consolidated statement with a number of annexes, and I should like to tender this under Rule 92 ter today. Perhaps the version as is can be tendered, and then once the text is redacted we could then substitute the amended version instead of the previous version. I'd like to add that we have prepared an index which will enable you to find the various annexes along with the ERN numbers and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The Chamber, isn't it. Then there's no need to explain that it does exist. Please proceed. And perhaps why just not put the 92 ter statement to the witness and seek the attestations needed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, that is exactly what I intended to do. The binder has been positioned on the witness's desk by the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, you have given a consolidated statement in June of 2007. The document that you have before you, does this correspond to the consolidated statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, could you indicate whether this reflects faithfully the testimony that you gave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, if the questions that were put to you at that session when you presented your consolidated statement were put to you again today, would you respond in same fashion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the 92 ter statement --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P618, marked for identification. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was initially 65 ter number ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number was to be determined. It has not been determined as of yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, we have a limited amount of time, and therefore I would like to ask you to be concise and to respond specifically to my questions, which is the only way that will enable us to deal with the essential questions that I would like to ask you in the time that is available. My first point that I'd like to discuss with you for reasons of context is as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that I would like to ask that the Exhibit 1517 be put on the e-court. This is Professor Dunjic's resume, his curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, as you read through this resume, as well as paragraphs of your statement, it's clear that you have been involved in the identification of war victims in the former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have limited time. Is there anything on the curriculum that is in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was just to introduce a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, if you just put the question. If there's no dispute about the curriculum, then just put the questions in addition to what is already on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall ask the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You are a professor of forensic medicine. How many forensic medicine professors are there at the University of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Of the ones currently working at the institute, there are six of us professors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In paragraph 10 of your statement, you indicate that you have published a recent article with Mark Skinner entitled identification of victims from two mass graves in Serbia. Could you tell us who Mark Skinner is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: He was an anthropologist who I got to know at Batajnica, or rather, at the Batajnica site where we exhumed large numbers of victims. He was there as a representative of the international organisation for the missing persons, and he was assigned to us as an assistant. He's an anthropologist from Canada, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Are you aware, Professor Dunjic, that Professor Skinner was an expert for the Defence in this case, Haradinaj et al.?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: My colleague, anthropologist, Professor Marija Djuric who worked with us at Glodjane, Batajnica, and elsewhere told me that she had been informed by Mr. Skinner that he was going to be a consultant in the Defence team -- for the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to go on to a second point that will involve a series of questions related to the crime scene in Radonjic in 1998. Was that the first time you had been to that crime scene in 1998, was that the first time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, you have stated that the forensic operations began at the canal on September 11th, 1998. This is indicated in paragraph 52 of your statement, and you left the canal around 3.00, 4.00 in the afternoon, as it is stated in paragraph 60 of your statement. My question is as follows: When you were at the canal at that time, given your former experience, given the fact that you're a specialist in forensic medicine, did you notice anything that might have made you think that this crime scene had been fabricated?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well when you said "fabricated," do you mean it had been staged in any way? No. If my understanding is correct, it had not been staged in any way. This was a locality where body parts could be seen next to the canal wall leading to Lake Radonjic. The bodies were partly covered by soil and other parts could be seen. It was not staged in any way. It was a site where the bodies were exhumed, recovered and exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will interpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will interpose the same objection interposed before with regard to the issue of fabrication and staging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dutertre, at the same time if you're talking about the crime scene and staging, then that could mean a lot of things. It could mean that it was suggested that the people died over there or that -- it could be a lot of things. So if you want to know whether there's any staging involved, you would have to know what then was staged. I mean, certainly I take it that it was not staged that these were dead bodies. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In paragraph 35 of your statement, which has been contested might I add, you have indicated -- and I shall read it in English, if we could perhaps have it on the screen as well using Sanction, you say: [In English] "In my opinion, I am sure that the MUP or the VJ, prior to our arrival at the site, had not removed any of the bodies or mortal remains from the site." [Interpretation] Could you tell us what led you to draw that conclusion, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The corpses which were visible were to be found at the very bottom of the canal and were largely covered by soil and mud. These body parts, which were subsequently exhumed, clearly showed that the bodies had been down there for long -- for a long time. It was quite visible that none of the forces present approached them, and the bodies could be seen from that part of the road which overlooked the canal wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody approached the bodies in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there, but it might be my insufficient knowledge of the English language. How I understand 35 is that the witness -- in the opinion of the witness, the MUP or the VJ, prior to their arrival, had not removed any of the bodies or -- so that some of them were taken away and therefore not there anymore. That's how I read 35. If that's the case, then the answer of the witness is not focusing on what 35 says. Do you have any knowledge of whether there had been more dead bodies there and that were removed before your arrival by the MUP or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bodies were there when we arrived at the site, and they were visually uncovered by the MUP forces which had informed the competent bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just talking about bodies that were not there anymore removed by anyone before your arrival. Do you have any knowledge of such a removal of bodies not being present anymore when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any such knowledge of bodies having been removed. We removed them once we exhumed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does this clarify paragraph 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was the reason for the objection, what was the basis of the prior knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we can move on, Mr. Dutertre. This has been settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I should like to go on now to the issue of autopsies, and I will have several questions. In paragraph 60 of your statement - and if we could use Sanction to have it on the screen, please, you state, and again I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "I had originally planned to do this work in Decane but the situation was too dangerous there. The UCK was very present in these areas which would have made our work very perilous." Could you tell us why it is that you made that statement. Where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: We received that information from the organs which were constantly present with us, that's to say the MUP. When we were supposed to do the exhumations, since I was in charge of that, I had to establish and choose the location where we would perform autopsies. The -- initially, Decani was chosen as the place where autopsies were to be carried out. However, as we arrived at the site in vehicles, representatives of the court and the MUP, we established that the situation was quite dangerous. It was impossible to secure the general area in order to be able to carry the -- carry out the exhumations there. As we arrived at the police station in Decani, we were told by the officers there that no suitable location could be found locally where autopsies could be performed. We decided to go to Djakovica, where in consultation with the local people we -- I apologise. Let me just add that throughout that time we had police escorts with us and that there was restricted movement after 1800 hours. We were able to move only with the police escorts, and that allowed us only to go to the site itself and back to where the autopsies were performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... regarding autopsies, and here I'd like to refer to paragraph 43 and 49 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started speaking before the translation was finished. That creates gaps in the transcript. Would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honours. In paragraphs 43 and 49, you have explained, and again I'd like to have these paragraphs on the screen with Sanction, you describe your method for the numbering of the bodies on site, that there was a label in the bag and outside the bag. My question relates to the traceability of the bodies during the autopsy. In paragraph 85, you say the following, and again I'd like to have that paragraph on the screen with Sanction: [In English] "Before opening a bag, we would first re-label the bag." [Interpretation] Could you tell us what you mean by "re-label." Does that mean that you're copying the same thing that was on the previous label or was the numbering system a different one. Could you please tell us that and then secondly explain why you proceeded in that way.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In order to maintain custody, the continuity of custody over the bodies, I explained to you already how we added the letter "R". We would put a certain number attached to the body inside the body-bag and into the pocket on the body-bag. In order to take a photograph of the body-bag, we would take the number from the pocket and place it on the body-bag before opening the body-bag itself in order to see and to show that the numbers matched. This was done so that once the body-bag was opened, whatever could be found there, pieces of clothing and personal effects, that they all be labelled with the same marking that was chosen for that particular body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd now like to discuss the various elements that were found with the bodies, found in the bags with the bodies. As regards body R-12, which is the sister of Witness SST07/04, which has -- has been proposed -- well, there's been a genetic examination in agreement with the Defence. I would like to call the 65 ter Exhibit number 867 on page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have not agreed to genetic examination with regard to R-12. That's an issue that's still open because we haven't received all of the underlying information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, how relevant is it for the questions to be put now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question does not relate to the identity. The only purpose of mentioning that was to identify the body for all parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... It's not. At this time, I think there's another way that he can get to the same information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, what you're seeking, Mr. Dutertre, is to get an explanation of these pictures and that's on the identity -- whether there's any agreement on the identity seems at this moment to be rather irrelevant for the questions you wanted to put, isn't it? First, I think it should not have been mentioned; second, it should not have been objected to at this moment, it could have been done at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, could you confirm, or rather, tell us what you see in the middle photograph. Perhaps we can have it enlarged for you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: This is a piece of barbed wire found next to the body R-12, and as we look at the top left-hand corner, we see the so-called sliding noose where one end is slipped through another one, a shorter one. In the bottom part of the photograph we can see a tangle of sorts. What you are showing now with the cursor is the sliding noose, and in the bottom part of the photograph we can see -- yes, exactly that part, we can see the remains of human hair. The remains of human hair that can be seen here are similar to the remains of human hair found on body marked as R-12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could you tell us what that means, that there be hair entwined in the barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise briefly to say paragraph 339 is out. I'm just making sure Mr. Dutertre knows that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I also said that if the -- this is not proper for introduction through 92 ter. What could still be asked and the question was rather unclear to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what it means --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: That's the point I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, if you put -- the objection against 339, of course, was what it led the witness to believe. If there's any inference to be drawn within the area of his competence, of course you could do so. But as it stands now, it certainly is an opinion which is -- as far as presented on paper is rather speculative. So therefore, if you can make it anything else, then please do so. But the question is not very appropriate to seek anything more than speculation. So therefore, if you would reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, how could you explain the presence here of hair on this barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It can be explained in the following way. This wire, especially with this form of sliding noose, must have been in contact with a person; or a person may have even been tied up with that barbed wire. That's the only possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question. Professor, you spoke about the hair being similar to the hair of R-12. What did you mean by "similar"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By saying that, I meant that the quality of the hair, its length and colour, matched the hair found on barbed wire here. This was established in an autopsy. We then checked whether this was the hair of R-12 or whether this hair was found here accidentally. What we established, however, was that the hair was of the same quality and of the same colour, and our conclusion was that it was similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I would object to this point, outside of his expertise, and I'm dealing with the issue of matching, for him to say the hair is similar, it's one issue; for him to say the hair is matching is an entirely different issue. There's an entire field of science that deals with hair samples and matching --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. Matching could mean several things, Mr. Guy-Smith, so therefore I would like to first explore it further. You said length, colour, and I think you said structure were similar. Was there anything you found which was not similar? So apart from the positive findings, was there an absence of any negative findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot recall now any negative findings. We were looking for things that approximately match one another. So based on similarity, this is the usual method of work in forensics. So it is an assumption. We did not determine the physiological origin or the DNA composition to be able to say: This does belong to the same person. But visually, macroscopically, which is part of the forensic expert's duties, led us to the conclusions that I have just presented to you. Thus there is similarity, but we are not asserting that it does come from that same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith, that means that within the criteria investigated there was a match, which means that identity may not have been established and at the same time there are no reasons at this moment to assume that they were not from the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are the conclusions, logical conclusions I would say, from this and I would like to invite Mr. Dutertre to continue but the word "match" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Has a very specific scientific meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A very, very specific scientific meaning. One of the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would appreciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At a later stage we will discuss the meaning of the word "match".

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I would appreciate obtaining the professor's working notes with regard to microscopic examinations which we have yet to receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, that's clear to you. I don't know whether it's anywhere in the exhibits, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I would like to, continue discussing the various elements found with the bodies. Body R-3 I don't believe there is any objection here. I think we've finalised. This is the body of Misin Berisha under -- under Count 19 and 20 of the indictment. You have indicated the following as regards this body: [In English] "There was a piece of yellow sticky tape found next to the corpse.". [Interpretation] I would like to call Exhibit 65 ter 856, page 21. Could we have this on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 867. Could the usher perhaps -- it's annex 186 of the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, is it -- is the yellow sticky tape that you referred to in paragraph 212 that we can see here on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you describe this sticky tape in further detail, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The sticky tape that was found with the body R-3 close to it is similar, even to say identical to the tape found next to body R-4. It's plastic sticky tape stuck several times, which in the middle part at the bottom where you can see, is a little bit thinner or worn down. So if I were to show you this paper, it's pinched together in its central part. I don't know if I'm being clear. Comparing the sticky tape and the other sticky tape from R-4, we concluded that the victims were both bound with the tape -- that their mouth was bound and the narrow part, worn-down part, in the middle of the sticky tape would correspond to the place where the victims bit down on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Same objection: Outside of the expertise of the witness, calls for a conclusion, and is speculative. With regard to -- with regard to not anything other than lines 9 through 13. The other part of the answer I have no difficulty with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I would like to discuss now, now that we've discussed the objects found with the victims, the injuries that you found on the bodies. R-4, first of all, and here I don't believe there are any objections as regards this body. I think that we're finalising, it's Zenun Gashi, this is Count 19 and 20. On paragraph 233 you stated that both arms were broken, were fractured, at the same level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps have this passage on the screen using Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In paragraph 234, you indicated that these injuries could not have been caused by a fall from the top of the embankment at the bottom of which the body was found. So I'm referring to paragraphs 233 and 234. While you're reading these paragraphs I would like to call Exhibit 1518 under Rule 65 ter. And perhaps we can go back to the e-court if you've -- if everyone has had time to read those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that page, it's the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next, next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the next. Again the next -- sorry, that's not the page I'm looking for. I apologise for wasting time, Your Honour. While we're looking for the right document, perhaps I could ask a question to the witness, which is as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is the meaning, from your point of view, of the fact that both arms were fractured at the same level?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to answer this question directly, and, Your Honours, I would just like to say that I am in a position as an expert -- expert in this field in my country and questions are being put to me and I'm expected to provide my expert opinion. But in view of a question which is being put to me in this way by the Prosecutor, I'm going to respond as an expert and I would not like that to be associated with any kind of free thinking of my own. Thus, with this witness we found fractures in the distal parts of both arms, as I'm indicating that now. In several cases that we had there that we processed, we found similar cases, similar fractures, identical, symmetrical fractures which led us to conclude, since we all discussed this: How could such a fracture be accused at the same height? And we came to the conclusion that it was probably a matter of the victims having their hands bound and then a strong blunt instrument acting at the same level at the same place. This is not a manipulation, it's an expert opinion in view of the nature of the injuries and in view of the fact that the body was found at a slope -- well, there is a slope. There is a concrete wall of the canal. The body was found at the bottom of the slope. A body falling or rolling down this slope cannot cause this injury. This injury can be caused only upon the direct action of a heavy blunt instrument as we would describe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, I'm looking at the clock. At the same time, I said yesterday the Chamber would very much like to conclude with this witness. I have asked the staff to see whether there's any possibility to have additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The feedback from those who would have to assist us to continue later today has not been received yet. But for practical purposes, Mr. Dutertre, how much time do you think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had asked a total of an hour and a half. I think -- well, a good half-hour will enable me to finish with this witness if I am concise and perhaps set aside a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour is too much at this moment to continue, and apart from that it would need consultation with the -- the Chamber who would be in this courtroom. Therefore, I think we are at least going to adjourn, Professor Dunjic, but the Chamber would very much like to see whether there's any possibility for that remaining half-hour to find the cooperation of all we would need to finish today rather than to -- to ask you to return at a later date. Because, as you know, Mr. Dutertre, the planning was to have the examination-in-chief done before we adjourned today, especially since the next hearing day would be the 16th of July. If there's no possibility to find another half an hour or one hour today, we need courtroom, we need interpreters, we need security, we need transcribers, et cetera, then the Chamber will consider whether the examination-in-chief will be completed just prior to the examination -- cross-examination. So therefore, whether we would ask the witness to come back now and then again for cross-examination, that might be a bit too much. Therefore, Professor Dunjic, you will be informed about what will happen. So there are three possibilities: Either we continue today, and that would mean that we would finish your examination-in-chief today, you would then be later called for cross-examination, that might take considerable time. Another possibility is that we would like to see you back soon to finish, to complete your examination-in-chief, and then later to be called for cross-examination. That is not an attractive way of proceeding. And finally the last option would be that just prior to being cross-examined that you would complete your examination-in-chief. You'll hear this afternoon what will be the case. Therefore, we adjourn at this moment, but usually one says sine die, without a date, but even without a time at this moment. If we will not continue today and -- then we will resume at Monday, the 16th of July, 9.00, Courtroom III. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no problem from the Prosecution's point, but we have -- I checked with the witness before. He's not actually available to come back because of vacation until the 20th of August for the re-examination -- the cross-examination and the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
